sections.heading: Strife’s bitter children
sections.summary: Strife gives birth to suffering, violence, lies and other troubles. A knowingly false oath brings especially great harm.

cards.label: Strife
cards.general: Conflict and hostility, imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She gives birth to the troubles listed here.

cards.label: Toil
cards.general: Hard, exhausting work.
cards.here: Painful Toil is one of Strife’s children.

cards.label: Troubles as children
cards.general: A poem can turn an idea or experience into a living being.
cards.here: Hunger, Lies and the other troubles become members of a divine family.

cards.label: Lawlessness
cards.general: Disregard for laws and proper behavior.
cards.here: Lawlessness and Ruin are close companions.

cards.label: Ruin
cards.general: Disaster, including the reckless blindness that can lead to it.
cards.here: Strife’s daughter Ruin stays close to Lawlessness.

cards.label: Oath
cards.general: A solemn promise or claim, made with divine powers as witnesses.
cards.here: Oath becomes a divine being who punishes deliberate false swearing.

sections.heading: Nereus, the truthful sea god
sections.translation:
Pontus, the Sea, fathered Nereus, truthful and free from lies,
the eldest of his children. They call him the Old Man
because he is trustworthy and gentle. He never forgets
what is right, and his thoughts are fair and kind.
Then Pontus joined with Gaia, the Earth, and fathered
mighty Thaumas, proud Phorcys, Ceto with her lovely cheeks,
and Eurybia, whose heart is as hard as unbreakable stone.
sections.summary: The Sea fathers honest, gentle Nereus. With Earth, he also has Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and strong-hearted Eurybia.

cards.label: Pontus
cards.general: The Sea imagined as a god.
cards.here: He fathers Nereus and, with Gaia, four more children.

cards.label: Nereus
cards.general: A gentle, truthful sea god, often called the Old Man of the Sea.
cards.here: He is Pontus’s eldest child and always respects what is right.

cards.label: Gaia
cards.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She and Pontus are the parents of Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and Eurybia.

cards.label: Thaumas
cards.general: A divine son of Sea and Earth.
cards.here: He is described as mighty.

cards.label: Phorcys
cards.general: A sea god, born from Sea and Earth.
cards.here: He is described as proud.

cards.label: Ceto
cards.general: A sea goddess, born from Sea and Earth.
cards.here: The poem praises her lovely cheeks.

cards.label: Eurybia
cards.general: A goddess, born from Sea and Earth.
cards.here: Her hard, unyielding spirit is compared to unbreakable stone.

sections.heading: Fifty daughters of the sea
sections.summary: Nereus and Doris have fifty sea-goddess daughters. Some calm waves and winds; all are skilled at their work.

cards.label: Nereids
cards.general: The fifty sea-goddess daughters of Nereus and Doris.
cards.here: The poem names all fifty and praises their beauty and skill.

cards.label: Nereus
cards.general: The truthful, gentle sea god introduced just before this passage.
cards.here: He is the father of all fifty daughters.

cards.label: Doris, the mother
cards.general: A goddess who is a daughter of Oceanus.
cards.here: She and Nereus are the parents of the fifty sea goddesses.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
cards.here: He is Doris’s father and the daughters’ grandfather.

cards.label: The sea that yields no harvest
cards.general: A poetic description of the sea, where people cannot grow crops.
cards.here: It sets the daughters’ home apart from cultivated land.

cards.label: Amphitrite
cards.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
cards.here: She helps Cymodoce and Cymatolege calm waves and winds.

cards.label: Thetis
cards.general: One of Nereus and Doris’s sea-goddess daughters.
cards.here: She appears near the beginning of the list.

cards.label: Doris, the daughter
cards.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
cards.here: She shares her name with her mother.

cards.label: Galatea
cards.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
cards.here: The poem singles out her beauty.

cards.label: Cymodoce
cards.general: A sea goddess whose name is connected with waves.
cards.here: She calms waves and fierce winds with two of her sisters.

cards.label: Cymatolege
cards.general: A sea goddess whose name suggests stilling waves.
cards.here: She helps Cymodoce and Amphitrite calm the sea.

cards.label: Rosy arms
cards.general: Arms whose beauty or color is compared to roses.
cards.here: The description praises Eunice and Hipponoe.

cards.label: Nemertes
cards.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
cards.here: She shares the mind of her truthful father, Nereus.

sections.heading: Swift wings and Medusa’s children
sections.translation:
Thaumas married Electra, daughter of deep-flowing Oceanus.
She gave birth to swift Iris, the rainbow goddess,
and the lovely-haired Harpies, winged beings named Aello and Ocypete.
On swift wings they keep pace with gusts of wind and birds,
racing high through the air.

Ceto bore Phorcys the lovely-cheeked Graeae,
gray-haired from birth. That is why immortal gods
and people walking the earth call them the Graeae—the Gray Women:
Pemphredo in her beautiful robe, and Enyo in a saffron-yellow robe.
She also bore the Gorgons, three fearsome sisters who live
beyond glorious Oceanus, at the world’s edge toward Night,
where the clear-voiced Hesperides, the maidens of evening, live:
Sthenno, Euryale and Medusa, who suffered a terrible fate.

Medusa was mortal; the other two could never die or grow old.
With her the dark-haired sea god Poseidon slept,
in a soft meadow among the flowers of spring.
When Perseus, a mortal hero, cut off her head,
mighty Chrysaor and Pegasus the horse sprang out.
Pegasus took his name from the Greek word for “springs,”
for he was born beside the springs of Oceanus;
Chrysaor’s name means “Golden Sword,” for he held a golden sword in his hands.

Pegasus flew away, leaving earth, the mother of sheep,
and reached the immortal gods. He lives in the halls of Zeus,
carrying thunder and lightning for that wise god.
sections.summary: Electra bears Iris and the Harpies. Ceto bears the Graeae and Gorgons. When Perseus kills Medusa, Chrysaor and Pegasus spring out; Pegasus flies to live with Zeus.

cards.label: Thaumas
cards.general: A divine son of Sea and Earth.
cards.here: He marries Electra and fathers Iris and the Harpies.

cards.label: Electra
cards.general: A goddess who is a daughter of Oceanus.
cards.here: She is the mother of Iris, Aello and Ocypete.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river imagined as circling the world.
cards.here: Electra is his daughter; the Gorgons live beyond him.

cards.label: Iris
cards.general: The goddess associated with the rainbow.
cards.here: She is the swift daughter of Thaumas and Electra.

cards.label: Harpies
cards.general: Winged female beings associated with rushing winds.
cards.here: They have lovely hair and fly as fast as winds and birds.

cards.label: Aello
cards.general: A Harpy whose name suggests a storm wind.
cards.here: She is one of Electra’s two Harpy daughters.

cards.label: Ocypete
cards.general: A Harpy whose name means “swift-flying.”
cards.here: She races through the air alongside Aello.

cards.label: Ceto and Phorcys
cards.general: Sea divinities, both children of Sea and Earth.
cards.here: They are the parents of the Graeae and the Gorgons.

cards.label: Graeae
cards.general: A name meaning “Gray Women.”
cards.here: These sisters have gray hair from the moment they are born.

cards.label: Pemphredo
cards.general: One of the Graeae.
cards.here: She wears a beautiful robe.

cards.label: Enyo
cards.general: One of the Graeae named in this passage.
cards.here: She wears a saffron-yellow robe.

cards.label: Saffron-yellow
cards.general: A rich yellow like the color produced by saffron, a flower-derived spice and dye.
cards.here: It describes Enyo’s robe.

cards.label: Gorgons
cards.general: Three fearsome sisters: Sthenno, Euryale and Medusa.
cards.here: They live beyond Oceanus, near Night.

cards.label: Night
cards.general: Darkness imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: Her region marks the remote edge of the world.

cards.label: Hesperides
cards.general: Divine maidens associated with evening and the far west.
cards.here: Their clear voices are heard in the region where the Gorgons live.

cards.label: Sthenno
cards.general: One of the three Gorgon sisters.
cards.here: She is immortal and never grows old.

cards.label: Euryale
cards.general: One of the three Gorgon sisters.
cards.here: Like Sthenno, she is immortal and never grows old.

cards.label: Medusa
cards.general: The only mortal Gorgon.
cards.here: Perseus cuts off her head, and Chrysaor and Pegasus spring out.

cards.label: Mortal and immortal
cards.general: A mortal can die; an immortal cannot.
cards.here: Medusa can die, while her two sisters cannot die or grow old.

cards.label: Poseidon
cards.general: The god of the sea.
cards.here: The poem calls him “Dark-haired” and says he slept with Medusa.

cards.label: Perseus
cards.general: A mortal hero in Greek myth.
cards.here: He kills Medusa by cutting off her head.

cards.label: Chrysaor
cards.general: A mythical figure whose name means “Golden Sword.”
cards.here: He springs from Medusa holding a golden sword.

cards.label: Pegasus
cards.general: A winged horse.
cards.here: He springs from Medusa, flies to the gods and carries Zeus’s thunder and lightning.

cards.label: Pegasus and springs
cards.general: Hesiod connects Pegasus’s name with pēgai, the Greek word for springs.
cards.here: The poem explains his name through his birthplace beside Oceanus’s springs.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the Greek gods, associated with thunder and lightning.
cards.here: Pegasus lives in his halls and carries his thunder and lightning.
